name: Soft drinks/carbonated beverages
anchor: Per-form sovereign beverage cells in the as-consumed liquid basis (EU 2023/915 juice and rice-drink cells, Codex CXS 193 fruit juices, EU 2024/1987 beverage nickel, EU canned-beverage tin, Hong Kong Cap 132V's named carbonated, tea, coffee and wine beverage entries, and the US and Hong Kong packaged-drinking-water quality standards), with dry leaf, bean and powder commodities anchored separately in their own as-sold basis and never converted between the two
native_basis_label: ready-to-drink liquid, as consumed (wet weight, single strength); a concentrate or a powder-to-liquid product is assessed as reconstituted to single strength per the manufacturer's own directions, which is the basis EU 2023/915 and Codex CXS 193 write into their juice cells and Hong Kong Cap 132V Note 11 writes into its beverage entries
scope_note: Ready-to-drink carbonated and still soft drinks: colas, lemon-lime and other flavoured carbonates, root beer, ginger ale, tonic water, bitter lemon, sodas containing a minor juice fraction, and their post-mix syrup and concentrate forms assessed as dispensed or reconstituted to the label dilution. Every packaging format including aluminium cans, PET, glass and post-mix bag-in-box. A carbonated water with no formulated load routes to the flavoured-water row; a sports, isotonic or energy formulation routes to the sports and energy drink row; a fruit juice or nectar routes to the juice rows; a fermented soft drink routes to the fermented-beverage row. This row is a FORMULATED ready-to-drink beverage, not water with flavour: the packaged-drinking-water quality standards relied on for the flavoured-water row are not applicable here, because the product carries a substantial dissolved load (sweetener systems, electrolyte salts, acidulants, stimulants, botanical extracts, colours and juice concentrates) that those instruments do not contemplate. The boundary is stated so the difference in published ceilings between this row and the flavoured-water row is legible as an applicability judgement rather than an inconsistency.
basis_guard: as[ _]consumed|wet weight|reconstituted|ready.to.drink|product as placed on market|\bjuice\b|single-strength|bottled water|portion ordinarily consumed
basis_guard_note: This row publishes a ready-to-drink liquid ceiling, so every named anchor must itself be written in a wet as-consumed (or as-placed-on-market liquid, or packaged-drinking-water) basis. The guard refuses any dry-commodity as-sold cell, any feed-basis cell, any food-contact migration limit and any article-content limit, because applying a dry leaf, bean or powder maximum level to a brewed or reconstituted liquid would be exactly the basis conflation Method v2.0 forbids. No brewing, dilution or reconstitution factor is invented in either direction.
method: HMTc Method v2.0 (government-limit-only): the strictest applicable sovereign maximum level for this exact beverage form and analyte in the row's declared native basis, with disclosed read-across where the exact cell is unregulated, a substantiated not-material determination where a species is bounded or is a method artifact, and a control where no defensible sovereign number and no supportable near-neighbour exist. Never occurrence-derived. Ready-to-drink and dry-commodity bases are never mixed and no brewing, dilution or reconstitution factor is invented.

Pb.basis: as consumed, ready-to-drink carbonated or still soft drink, or concentrate as dispensed or reconstituted to the label dilution (read across from the Hong Kong carbonated-beverage cell)
Pb.label: Hong Kong Cap 132V Part 2 item 9 sets lead in Carbonated beverages at 0.2 mg/kg = 200 ug/kg, with Note 11 scoping the cell to beverages that are, or are reconstituted to be, ready to drink. That cell directly governs the carbonated forms in this row and is the nearest applicable sovereign value for the still soft drinks the row also admits, which share the formulation, the process and the packaging but not the carbonation. It is adopted by disclosed read-across so that a single ceiling governs both forms.
Pb.substantiation: The provenance is recorded as read-across and not as regulatory-alignment because this row's scope is wider than the instrument's. For a cola, a tonic water or a ginger ale the Hong Kong cell is a direct sovereign maximum level for the exact product form; for a still soft drink it is the nearest applicable analog, and the tag follows the weaker of the two rather than the stronger. The sibling sports and energy drink row adopts the same anchor for the same still and carbonated mix and carries the same tag, so the two rows are consistent on their face. Three disclosures belong here. First, no other credible sovereign regulates this product form at all: the EU, Codex, FSANZ and Health Canada write no soft-drink lead cell, so 200 ug/kg is the whole of the applicable law and there is no stricter applicable value to select. Second, the stricter beverage cells that exist are inapplicable and were rejected as such rather than quietly ignored: the EU and Codex fruit-juice cells (30 ug/kg) are scoped to fruit juices, juices from concentrate and nectars, which a cola carrying a few percent juice is not, and the packaged-drinking-water quality standards (5 to 10 ug/kg) govern water sold as water. HMTc will not reach past an instrument's scope to publish a better-looking number. Third, HMTc does not pretend 200 ug/kg is a strong ceiling: this cell is a declared Standards Ratchet priority, and Governance Policy section 12 is the only route by which certified-lot evidence may lower it.

companions.scope: fruit juices, fruit juices from concentrate, concentrated fruit juices,

companions.basis: food as listed in Cap 132V Part 2 Schedule; source unit mg/kg
companions.scope: Fruit juices, other than fruit juices exclusively from berries and other

Cd.rationale: No credible sovereign sets a cadmium maximum level for a soft drink or carbonated beverage. No credible sovereign sets a cadmium maximum level for any formulated non-alcoholic beverage; the EU 2023/915 cadmium cells are commodity cells and the only beverage cadmium values in existence are the packaged-drinking-water standards, which govern water sold as water. No near-neighbour read-across is supportable, so the fail-safe disposition is a control: cadmium testing is mandatory on every certified lot and no ceiling is invented from occurrence data.
Cd.reference_method: Cadmium by ICP-MS on every certified lot, reported on the certificate. A result above 10 ug/kg in a ready-to-drink form, or above 100 ug/kg in a dry form, escalates to an ingredient-origin and process-water investigation and is a Standards Ratchet surveillance input under Governance Policy section 12.

tAs.rationale: No credible sovereign sets a total-arsenic maximum level for a soft drink or carbonated beverage. Regulators write beverage arsenic limits on the inorganic species (EU 2023/915 section 3.4.4 fruit juices at 20 ug/kg and section 3.4.1.6 non-alcoholic rice-based drinks at 30 ug/kg; the US FDA apple-juice action level at 10 ug/kg) and write unspeciated arsenic limits only in the packaged-water and public-water-supply schedules, which are Category 8 instruments. The inorganic-arsenic cell in this row carries the health-relevant fraction. Total arsenic is therefore mandatory on every lot as the parent screen and no total-arsenic ceiling is invented.
tAs.reference_method: Total arsenic by ICP-MS on every certified lot. Inorganic-arsenic speciation (HPLC-ICP-MS) is reflexed whenever total arsenic exceeds 50 percent of this row's inorganic-arsenic ceiling, or 20 ug/kg where this row publishes no inorganic-arsenic number. Species never substitute for the total: the iAs result does not satisfy the tAs reporting requirement.

iAs.basis: wet weight, ready-to-drink beverage (read across from the EU fruit-juice inorganic-arsenic cell)
iAs.source_scope: fruit juices, concentrated fruit juices as reconstituted, and fruit nectars
iAs.label: No credible sovereign has written an inorganic-arsenic maximum level for a soft drink. The EU 2023/915 section 3.4.4 fruit-juice cell (20 ug/kg) is the strictest sovereign inorganic-arsenic value written for any ready-to-drink beverage and is adopted by disclosed read-across in the identical liquid basis.
iAs.substantiation: Beverage-to-beverage read-across with no basis change, adopted in the strict direction because the alternative was no ceiling at all. Arsenic reaches a soft drink through process water, acidulants, colours and juice or extract fractions, all of which an aqueous beverage cell at 20 ug/kg contemplates. The rice-drink cell (30 ug/kg) is looser and scoped to a rice hazard this row does not carry; the apple-juice action level (10 ug/kg) is scoped to a single named commodity.

tHg.rationale: No credible sovereign sets a total-mercury maximum level for a soft drink or carbonated beverage. The sovereign mercury values in this basis family are the packaged-drinking-water quality standards (US 21 CFR 165.110 total mercury at 2 ug/kg; Hong Kong Cap 132V packaged drinking water, written for inorganic mercury at 6 ug/kg) and the fish and seafood methylmercury and total-mercury ceilings, none of which governs this product form. Mercury has no identified enrichment pathway in this supply chain, but the analyte is on the mandatory eight-total panel, so testing is mandatory and no ceiling is invented.
tHg.reference_method: Total mercury by ICP-MS (or dedicated amalgamation AAS) on every certified lot, reported on the certificate. A detection above 5 ug/kg escalates to an ingredient and process-water investigation and reflexes methylmercury speciation.

MeHg.rationale: Methylmercury has no formation pathway in a soft drink or carbonated beverage: there is no marine bioaccumulation step in the supply chain and no anaerobic, sulfate-reducing methylation environment in the product or its process. Methylmercury is a component of total mercury (MeHg <= tHg) and is governed by and bounded by the total-mercury cell; no separate methylmercury ceiling is published.
MeHg.reference_method: Bounded by the total-mercury cell (tHg). Methylmercury speciation (HPLC-ICP-MS or GC-ICP-MS) is reflexed only on an elevated total-mercury result; it is not a routine lot test for this form.
MeHg.regulatory_basis: No credible sovereign sets a methylmercury limit for any beverage, leaf, bean or beverage powder. Methylmercury maximum levels are scoped to fish, seafood and other marine matrices (EU 2023/915 section 3.3, US FDA CPG 540.600, Hong Kong Cap 132V fish entries). Methylmercury is a species of and bounded by total mercury (MeHg <= tHg), which this row controls directly.
MeHg.jurisdictions_checked: EU 2023/915 (and EU 2024/1987 for nickel, EU 2025/1891 for arsenic in seafood); Codex CXS 193-1995; US FDA (21 CFR 165.110 bottled-water quality standards, Juice HACCP guidance, Closer to Zero action levels); FSANZ Food Standards Code Schedule 19; Health Canada List of Contaminants and Other Adulterating Substances; UK retained maximum levels; Hong Kong Cap 132V (Food Adulteration (Metallic Contamination) Regulations) — none sets a methylmercury limit for this product form.

Ni.basis: product as placed on market, ready-to-drink beverage (read across from the EU beverage nickel cell)
Ni.label: No credible sovereign has written a nickel maximum level for a soft drink. EU 2024/1987's fruit and vegetable juices and nectars cell (250 ug/kg) is the only sovereign nickel value written for a ready-to-drink beverage and is adopted by disclosed read-across in the identical liquid basis.
Ni.substantiation: Beverage-to-beverage read-across with no basis change. Nickel in a soft drink is a stainless-plant, process-water and mineral-salt signal. The Hong Kong packaged-water nickel cell (70 ug/kg) is stricter but governs water sold as water and is inapplicable to a formulated beverage. Nickel is a Tier-2 analyte.

Sn.basis: product as placed on market, ready-to-drink liquid (inorganic tin)
Sn.label: EU 2023/915 Annex I section 3.5.2 sets inorganic tin in canned beverages, including canned fruit and vegetable juices, at 100 mg/kg = 100000 ug/kg; Hong Kong Cap 132V sets canned beverages at 150000 ug/kg. The EU value is the strictest applicable and binds. This is a direct sovereign maximum level on the beverage-in-a-can form, not a read-across.
Sn.substantiation: Tin in a beverage is a tinplate and can-lining migration pathway, so the government instruments are written on the canned form and the canned form is where the hazard sits. The EU cell (100000 ug/kg) directly governs every canned or tinplate-packaged product in this row and is adopted as the row ceiling for all packaging formats; a carton, PET, glass or pouch format has no tin source and complies trivially, so no separate non-canned cell is published. The looser Hong Kong canned-beverage cell (150000) and the canned-foods cells for solid foods (EU 200000; Codex, FSANZ and Hong Kong 250000) are disclosed and deliberately not adopted: EU writes a stricter cell specifically for beverages and HMTc preserves that product-form split. Tin is a Tier-2 analyte; an elevated result in a non-canned format is a packaging-integrity signal.

Al.rationale: No credible sovereign sets an aluminium maximum level for a soft drink or carbonated beverage. The only sovereign aluminium values in a dietary basis are the packaged-drinking-water quality standards (US 21 CFR 165.110 secondary allowable level 200 ug/kg, EU 2020/2184, Health Canada 2900 ug/kg), which govern water sold as water and are Category 8 instruments, and the FSANZ infant-formula aluminium limits, which are Category 1 and are excluded from this category's anchor set by the taxonomy boundary rule. In this form aluminium is a packaging and processing signal (aluminium cans and can linings, closures, filter aids, additive carry-over) rather than a raw-material contaminant. Aluminium is a live cell for this row because the dominant packaging format is the aluminium can and because a low-pH carbonated formulation is exactly the condition under which a compromised can lining leaches, so the tripwire is a packaging-integrity control as well as an ingredient control.
Al.reference_method: Total aluminium by ICP-MS on every certified lot, reported on the certificate. A result that departs materially from the applicant's own documented process baseline escalates to a packaging, can-lining and processing-aid investigation. This is a process-control tripwire, not a numeric standard: no ceiling is published because no credible sovereign maximum exists for this cell.

Cr.rationale: No credible sovereign sets a total-chromium maximum level for a soft drink or carbonated beverage. The only sovereign chromium values reachable from this basis family are the packaged-drinking-water quality standards (US 21 CFR 165.110 at 100 ug/kg, Hong Kong Cap 132V packaged drinking water at 50 ug/kg), which govern water sold as water and are Category 8 instruments, and the public-water-system maximum contaminant levels (US EPA, Health Canada), which are water-utility instruments and not food law at all. Total chromium in this form is dominated by benign Cr(III) and is reported as a stainless-steel equipment and process-water leaching screen, not as a health limit; the health-relevant species is addressed in the Cr-VI cell.
Cr.reference_method: Total chromium by ICP-MS on every certified lot, reported on the certificate. An elevated result triggers the Cr(VI) speciation reflex and an equipment, process-water and ingredient investigation.

Cr-VI.rationale: Hexavalent chromium is not stable in a carbonated or still soft drink. At the pH of this product form (typically pH 2.4 to 3.5, with phosphoric, citric and carbonic acid and invert or high-fructose sugars present in the formulation) Cr(VI) is reduced to Cr(III) by the organic acids, sugars, ascorbate and polyphenols present in the matrix, so a positive Cr(VI) result is an artifact of the total-chromium determination rather than a species present in the beverage as consumed. The reference-method basis for this determination is the in-house species arbitration at data/workbench/standards/2026-07-31-chromium-formula-adjudication.md, which found that the superseded ion-exchange plus electrothermal-AAS methods that generated the historical Cr(VI) values in liquid food matrices are not reproduced by the modern reference method: saraiva2021 (species-specific isotope dilution HPLC-ICP-MS, limit of quantification 0.049 ug/kg) quantified no Cr(VI) in any milk or formula sample while resolving Cr(III) and total chromium at single-digit ug/kg. That adjudication was drawn on a near-neutral aqueous food matrix; the acidic beverage matrices in this row are a more strongly reducing environment still, so the artifact conclusion carries a fortiori. The health-relevant species is controlled through the total-chromium cell and the reflex rule below, and this determination is a method finding, not an occurrence-derived value: no number is taken from it.
Cr-VI.reference_method: Hexavalent chromium is not a routine lot test. Total chromium (Cr cell) bounds any hexavalent fraction; a Cr(VI)-specific method (IC-ICP-MS, EN 15192 adapted to the liquid matrix) is reflexed where the total-chromium screen is elevated AND the finished-product pH is above 5.0, and a confirmed detection blocks certification pending a process and equipment investigation.
Cr-VI.regulatory_basis: No credible sovereign sets a hexavalent-chromium content limit for any food or beverage; every sovereign chromium value in a dietary or packaged-water basis is written for total chromium (US 21 CFR 165.110 chromium 100 ug/kg; Hong Kong Cap 132V packaged drinking water 50 ug/kg). Cr(VI) is a species of and bounded by total chromium (Cr-VI <= total Cr).
Cr-VI.jurisdictions_checked: EU 2023/915 (and EU 2024/1987 for nickel, EU 2025/1891 for arsenic in seafood); Codex CXS 193-1995; US FDA (21 CFR 165.110 bottled-water quality standards, Juice HACCP guidance, Closer to Zero action levels); FSANZ Food Standards Code Schedule 19; Health Canada List of Contaminants and Other Adulterating Substances; UK retained maximum levels; Hong Kong Cap 132V (Food Adulteration (Metallic Contamination) Regulations) — none sets a hexavalent-chromium limit for a food or beverage.
